title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 5: Establishing the Business Requirement

questions.question: Which level of requirements is the highest level of abstraction?
questions.explanation: Business requirements are the top-level requirements. User and functional requirements are subordinate to them.

questions.question: User requirements and functional requirements should support the project's business objectives.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that lower-level requirements should not be included if they do not address the business objectives.

questions.question: Why is it important for stakeholders to share the same understanding of business objectives?
options: So all stakeholders use the same programming language
So project participants do not work against each other
So developers can avoid talking to users
So every feature receives equal priority
questions.explanation: A shared understanding of business objectives helps keep project participants aligned instead of pulling the project in conflicting directions.

questions.question: According to the lecture, business requirements consist mainly of which two components?
questions.explanation: The professor emphasizes that business requirements consist primarily of product vision and project scope.

questions.question: What does the product vision describe?
options: The ultimate long-term goal of the product
The exact functionality of the next release
questions.explanation: The product vision describes the long-term direction or ultimate goal for the product.

questions.question: The product vision generally changes slowly over time.
questions.explanation: Because it represents the long-term goal, the product vision is relatively stable compared with the project scope.

questions.question: What does project scope primarily describe?
options: The long-term future of the company
The short-term objective and which part of the vision will be addressed now
questions.explanation: Scope identifies the portion of the broader product vision that a particular project or release will address.

questions.question: A project's scope typically covers:
options: Every release the product will ever have
questions.explanation: The slides state that project scope normally applies to one product release.

questions.question: Which constraints can cause project scope to be adjusted? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Scope must adapt to practical constraints such as cost, schedule, resources, quality, and available capacity.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the difference between vision and scope?
options: Vision is short-term while scope is long-term
Vision defines the long-term product direction, while scope defines what part of that vision is addressed in the current project or release
Vision describes source code while scope describes tests
Vision and scope mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Vision describes where the product is ultimately going; scope defines what the current project will actually tackle.

questions.question: Requirements conflicts among stakeholders are normal.
questions.explanation: Different stakeholders naturally have different priorities, so conflicts should be expected and managed.

questions.question: Which stakeholder preference is matched correctly?
questions.explanation: The slides associate managers with predictability and profit.

questions.question: Which pair correctly reflects common stakeholder interests from the slides?
options: Customer wants simplicity; user wants convenience and features
Customer wants maximum technical complexity; user wants fewer features
Developer wants predictability; manager wants experimental technology
Sponsor wants no decisions; user wants funding control
Manager wants simplicity; customer wants source code
Developer wants fewer features; user wants lower staffing
questions.explanation: The chapter uses this contrast to show why business requirements can conflict.

questions.question: Who is responsible for resolving conflicts involving business stakeholders?
questions.explanation: The sponsor is responsible for resolving business-level conflicts when stakeholders cannot all be satisfied.

questions.question: Why can stakeholder conflict not always be solved by satisfying everyone?
options: Because stakeholders can have competing goals and constraints
Because the project scope never matters
Because customers do not influence requirements
questions.explanation: Different stakeholders can have incompatible priorities, so tradeoffs are often required.

questions.question: Business requirements can influence which aspects of use cases? Select all that apply.
options: How many use cases are included
How extensively a use case is implemented
The priority of each use case
Which business goals the use cases support
Whether a use case belongs in the release
questions.explanation: Business requirements guide which use cases are included, how much of them is implemented, and their relative priority.

questions.question: A use case that does not support any business objective should automatically be included because users requested it.
questions.explanation: Lower-level requirements should align with the business requirements and defined scope.

questions.question: How many vision and scope documents should normally exist for the project, even if multiple systems will be developed?
options: A single vision and scope document
None if the project is large
questions.explanation: The slides state that there should be one vision and scope document even when several systems are involved.

questions.question: Who owns the vision and scope document?
questions.explanation: The project sponsor, such as an executive or funding authority, owns the vision and scope document.

questions.question: Who may provide input into the vision and scope document? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The document is owned by the sponsor, but input may come from many stakeholders and subject-matter experts.

questions.question: Which item belongs in the Business Requirements section of the vision and scope document?
questions.explanation: Business opportunity is one of the listed subsections of the Business Requirements section.

questions.question: Which of the following belong in the Business Requirements section? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: All six are included in the document outline shown in the slides.

questions.question: Business assumptions and dependencies belong under which section of the vision and scope document?
questions.explanation: They are listed under the Business Requirements section.

questions.question: Which item belongs under Scope and Limitation?
questions.explanation: Major features are included in the Scope and Limitation portion of the vision and scope document.

questions.question: Which of the following belong under Scope and Limitation? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: These four items define what is and is not included in the current and future project scope.

questions.question: Why are limitations and exclusions useful in a scope document?
options: They clearly state what the project will not include
They eliminate the need for requirements
They make all future changes impossible
questions.explanation: Explicitly documenting exclusions helps prevent misunderstandings and scope creep.

questions.question: Which item belongs under Business Context?
questions.explanation: Stakeholder profiles are part of the Business Context section.

questions.question: Stakeholder profiles can include which information? Select all that apply.
options: Value the stakeholder expects from the product
How the stakeholder relates to the product
questions.explanation: The slides describe stakeholder profiles in terms of value, attitude, features of interest, and other relevant business interests.

questions.question: Project priorities are described in terms of:
options: Constraints, drivers, and degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: The Business Context section includes project priorities expressed through constraints, drivers, and degrees of freedom.

questions.question: Which items may be considered deployment considerations? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: These are the deployment considerations listed in the slides.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a context diagram?
options: To show the system and how it interacts with external entities through information flows
To show only internal database tables
questions.explanation: A context diagram gives a high-level picture of the system boundary, external entities, and exchanged information.

questions.question: In a context diagram, the main system is shown together with:
questions.explanation: The diagram shows the system in relation to external entities and the information exchanged with them.

questions.question: In the Chemical Tracking System example, the chemist sending a request for a chemical to the system is an example of:
options: An information flow between an external entity and the system
questions.explanation: The professor uses this example to explain how context diagrams show external entities exchanging data with the system.

questions.question: What does an ecosystem map primarily show?
options: How the system's related components or subsystems interact with one another
questions.explanation: An ecosystem map provides a broader graphical view of related systems or components and their interactions.

questions.question: A context diagram and an ecosystem map are exactly the same representation.
questions.explanation: A context diagram emphasizes the system boundary and exchanges with external entities, while an ecosystem map shows the wider network of interacting systems or components.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a feature tree?
options: To decompose major product features into smaller supporting features
questions.explanation: A feature tree breaks larger capabilities into smaller related sub-features.

questions.question: The lecture describes a feature tree as a form of step-by-step refinement from larger abstractions to smaller ones.
questions.explanation: The professor explicitly explains feature decomposition as refining a larger abstraction into smaller supporting abstractions.

questions.question: In the Chemical Tracking System feature tree, 'Order Chemicals' is an example of:
options: A major feature that can be broken into sub-features
questions.explanation: The lecture uses 'Order Chemicals' as an example of a major feature that is decomposed into smaller features.

questions.question: Why is breaking a large feature into smaller sub-features useful?
options: It helps explain what smaller capabilities are needed to accomplish the larger feature
It guarantees the project has no defects
It eliminates the need for scope
It allows developers to ignore stakeholders
questions.explanation: Feature decomposition helps analysts understand the smaller capabilities required to realize a larger business capability.

questions.question: What is scope creep?
questions.explanation: Scope creep occurs when more and more functionality is added without disciplined scope control.

questions.question: Keeping scope under control means refusing all new requirements.
questions.explanation: The chapter says teams should prevent uncontrolled scope creep while still accommodating evolving needs.

questions.question: What are the three possible decisions for a newly proposed requirement? Select all that apply.
options: It is in scope, so keep it
It is out of scope, so discard it
It is out of scope but valuable enough to justify changing the scope
Always delay it until the next project
questions.explanation: The slides give exactly these three possible decisions for evaluating a proposed requirement against the project's scope.

questions.question: A proposed feature does not fit the current scope but strongly supports the business objectives. What is one valid response?
options: Change the project scope through an appropriate decision process
Ignore all cost and schedule impact
Ask the developer to build it without approval
questions.explanation: If an out-of-scope requirement is valuable enough, the project may deliberately change its scope rather than allowing uncontrolled scope creep.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes Chapter 5?
options: Business requirements define the long-term vision and current project scope, align lower-level requirements with business objectives, and provide techniques for documenting and controlling scope
Business requirements are mainly about source code architecture
The chapter focuses only on user interface design
The chapter explains how to eliminate all requirement conflicts
The chapter focuses entirely on testing
Business requirements apply only after implementation
questions.explanation: Chapter 5 is about establishing the top-level business requirements through product vision, project scope, supporting documentation, scope models, and scope control.
